h1: Starting a whisky collection in India on a sensible budget
title: Starting a Whisky Collection in India | Craft Beer School
desc: How to start a whisky collection in India on a sensible budget: what to buy first, how to store bottles in heat, buying safely and staying within the rules.
teaser: A good collection starts with whiskies you want to drink, bought one thoughtful bottle at a time.
standfirst: Collecting whisky does not need a big budget or rare bottles. It needs a plan, a cool cupboard and a bit of discipline about why you are buying each bottle.
sections: Decide what kind of collector you are

There are two kinds of collection. A drinking collection is a shelf of open bottles you taste, compare and share. An investment collection is sealed bottles held in the hope they rise in value. Most people are better off with the first. Whisky prices can fall as well as rise and sealed bottles earn nothing on the shelf.

Building a drinking collection teaches you far more. Every bottle you open sharpens your palate and helps you choose the next one well.

Aim for variety rather than age or price. A good starter shelf covers:

  • A light, fruity single malt matured mainly in ex-bourbon casks.
  • A sherry matured whisky for dried fruit and spice.
  • A peated whisky for smoke.
  • An Indian single malt to taste what heat does to maturation.
  • A bourbon or rye for new oak and different grains.
  • A good blend for everyday drinking and highballs.

Six styles side by side teach you more than six bottles from one region. Our guide to whisky styles of the world helps you pick.

Price on its own tells you little. Learn to read the label for the age statement, cask type, strength and whether the whisky is chill filtered or coloured. Our guide to whisky label terms covers the vocabulary.

Be careful with age. An age statement shows the youngest whisky in the bottle, but whiskies without one can still be excellent. Our guide to age statements explains why some very good whiskies carry no number.

Heat and light are the enemies. Store bottles upright, so the spirit does not eat into the cork, in a dark cupboard away from outer walls, kitchens and windows. A steady room temperature is better than a fridge. Avoid lofts and car boots in summer.

Keep the boxes or tubes. They block light and protect labels from humidity during the monsoon. If a cork dries out and crumbles, replace it with a clean spare stopper rather than leaving the bottle open.

Buy from licensed retail outlets and keep your bills. Counterfeit and refilled bottles exist, especially for famous names. Check seals, excise labels, fill levels and print quality. Be wary of prices that look too good.

Alcohol rules differ across India. Some states limit how much you can keep at home or need a permit to hold larger quantities. Carrying bottles across state lines can also be restricted. Travellers have a limited duty-free allowance when entering India. Rules vary by state and change, so check the current position before you stock up or travel with bottles.

Open your bottles. Taste each new one alongside one you know, add a few drops of water and write down what you find. A notebook or a simple spreadsheet becomes a record of how your palate develops.

Share with friends at a small, responsible tasting. You get to taste their bottles too. The collection grows in knowledge without growing in cost.

Before you chase new bottles, learn what you actually like. Pour two whiskies you own side by side and decide which you prefer and why. Is it the smoke, the fruit, the sweetness or the texture? Do this a few times and a pattern appears. You may find you prefer sherry casks to peat, or lighter malts to heavy ones.

That self-knowledge saves money. It stops you buying a famous bottle you will not enjoy and points you towards the styles that reward you. It also makes conversations with other collectors and shop staff far more useful, because you can describe what you want in words they understand.

Add one bottle at a time, each with a reason: a new style, a new cask type or a direct comparison with something you own. A collection of fifteen bottles you understand beats fifty you have never opened.

Miniatures of 50 ml or sample sets let you try a whisky before committing to a full bottle. They cost more per millilitre but save you from a 750 ml mistake. Swapping samples with friends who collect is another good way to taste widely on a modest budget.
faqs: How much should I spend on my first whisky bottles?
There is no fixed figure. Start with well-made bottles you can find again, so you can rebuy what you like. Variety teaches more than price.
Is whisky a good investment in India?
It is uncertain. Prices can fall and rules on holding and selling alcohol vary by state. Most people get more from a collection they drink and share.
Should whisky bottles be stored lying down?
No. Store them upright. High strength spirit can damage a cork that stays in contact with it.
